segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To call in Spanish, so to call to somebody and also to to make a phone call, is llamar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ll, and we said this double l creates a 'y' sound in most Spanish dialects just like the 'y'. Ll a m a r, llamar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And we said that in Spanish you don't tend to say "my name is" or "I am called", you say "I call myself" to introduce yourself. So how would you say "I call myself"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me llamo. Good. And if you want to ask somebody what their name is, you can say, "How do you call yourself?" So let's do this informally: "How do you call yourself?" What was the word for "how"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cómo. How do you call yourself?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Cómo te llamas? How would you say, "How does she call herself? What is her name?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Cómo se llama? Imagine you heard her name once before, and you wanted to say, "What was she called? How was she calling herself?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Cómo se llamaba? What was her name? What was his name? Or what was your name, formally? What was their name? What were they calling themselves?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Cómo se llamaban? Good. What was "to have" not in the sense of haber, not the have that we use to go into the past, but the have that we use for possession?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tener. Good. And we said also that this tener is the -tain, -tain, that we get inside various English verbs, or Latin English verbs like "contain": contain is contener. So we have this trick using tener that we can convert over some more verbs from English. So doing the same with "obtain", we would get?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Obtener. "Maintain", changed a little bit. Have a go.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mantener. We said that man- actually is like from mano, hand. "Sustain", this one changed a little bit as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sostener. So this -tain that we have in English is is tener, to have. So how would you say, "I used to have"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tenía. Good. So if you wanted to say, "I used to have a big house"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tenía un grande casa, un casa grande.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. These bits and pieces require a little thought as well. Tenía una casa grande. "We used to have a big house"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Teníamos una grande una casa grande.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Teníamos una casa grande. And the accent stays in the same place on the 'i-a', tenía, teníamos. Good. "I used to have four, but now I don't have any left. I used to have four, but now I don't have any left." The word for "four" is cuatro, cuatro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. So, "I used to have four"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I don't have any left", so "they don't remain me" or "it doesn't remain to me". That's all we need to say to give that "I don't have any left".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So all together: "I used to have four, but now I don't have any left."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Tenía cuatro, pero ahora no me queda.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tenía cuatro, pero ahora no me queda. Or, pero ahora no me quedan. You could use either. So we're not using have to give this meaning have left. How was "I have" in the present?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tengo. And how did you make that "I have to"? I have to in the sense of I must.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I have to see you", and let's speak informally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tengo que verte. Now if you want to say, "I had to see you", you can use this line in the past that we learned. Even though in English we're saying "had", not "having to", this is fine in Spanish. So, "I had to see you / I was having to see you"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tenía que verte. Good. "Yesterday" is ayer. A y e r, ayer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, "I had to see you yesterday"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Tenía que verte ayer. "To do" or "to make" was hacer. H a c e r, hacer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Did you have to do it yesterday? Talking informally. Did you have to do it yesterday?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Tenías que hacerlo ayer? Didn't you have to do it yesterday?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And and you could use this like, weren't you supposed to do it? ¿No tenías que hacerlo ayer? Didn't you have to do it yesterday? Weren't you supposed to do it yesterday? Good. I want to look at just three irregular verbs that we have for this line in the past. Now this is a very regular tense. There are very few irregularities in this tense. It's a very safe tense. And the irregularities that we have are with very small verbs. For example, ver. How was "I see" from ver?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Veo. The same irregularity that we get in the "I" form in the present, veo, we get it in this line in the past. So instead of taking off -er and putting -ía, we ended up with this extra 'e'. So, veía is "I was seeing / I used to see", "he was seeing / he used to see", "she was seeing / she used to see", or "you", formal, veía. Give me the the other versions then. "We were seeing"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Another irregular verb in this tense is ser. Ser, to be. Now the base for I, he, she, it, you formal is era. Era. Now this is very easy to remember because we are looking at the past which is a line in time, and an "era" in English is a line in time in the past. So we can just think of an era. We would use this with characteristic things. So for example, if you wanted to say, "I used to be a student", what was "student"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say, "I used to be a student"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Era estudiante. Good. We don't need the word for "a". Era estudiante. Good. "Were you a student?", informally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Where are you putting the accent? I couldn't tell.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I put it at the 'a', at the -amos, but it's éramos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Éramos, good. In these tenses, the accent doesn't move around. Good. So era, éramos. Good. "We were students"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "What were they? What were they?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. ¿Qué eran? Good. And then the last one of course that is irregular in this tense is ir. Ir, to go. Now, "I was going" is kind of like a blend of the two different ways we have of creating this past: -aba and -ía. "I was going" is iba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you see we get a bit of -ía and a bit of -aba with ir. "I was going" from "to go": iba. So, you can give me the other versions: "we were going"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now iba is very useful because, of course, you can use it like in the English "I was going to call you", for example. "I was going to go, but I didn't have the time. I was going to do it, but I forgot." So you can use it in this way as well, which is very common. So how would you say, "I was going to call you", and we are talking informally, "I was going to call you"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Iba, I was, I was going...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mm. What kind of verb is "going"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good! Iba a llamarte. "I was going to do it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And I'm not sure here if you're putting the 'a' to connect the verbs.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: If I did it? Yeah. No, I didn't. I forgot.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Iba a hacerlo. So actually in fluent speech, you would hear "iba hacerlo", all of those three a's: iba, a, hacer, will blend together, so that's why I wasn't sure if you said it or not. "We were going to do it / make it"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Íbamos a hacerlo. "We were going to do them / make them"?
